Cannabis on the Ballot: How Elections Shape the Rules Where You Live

Michigan legalized cannabis at the ballot box, and local votes still decide where stores can open. Here is who decides what, how to vote in Michigan, and how to keep election night calm.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20269 min read

09min readNews & Culture
In this article
  1. Why elections matter for cannabis policy at every level
  2. Michigan's ballot history: the 2008 medical vote and the 2018 adult-use vote
  3. Who decides what: Congress, state law, city councils
  4. Local opt-ins and opt-outs: how towns decide where dispensaries open
  5. Registering and voting in Michigan: deadlines, same-day registration, absentee and early voting
  6. Election day logistics
  7. A calm, responsible election-night watch party
  8. Picking a mood for the night without health claims
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • Michigan voters approved medical marijuana in 2008 and adult use in 2018, both through citizen-initiated ballot measures.
  • Congress and federal agencies set federal law, the state sets the statewide framework, and each city, village or township decides whether licensed stores may open.
  • In Michigan you can register in person at your clerk's office through 8 p.m. on Election Day, vote early in person for at least nine days, or vote absentee for any reason.
  • Cannabis use is not allowed in public places, including at the polls, and driving while impaired is against the law.

Cannabis on the ballot is how Michigan got legal cannabis in the first place. Voters, not lawmakers, approved medical marijuana in 2008 and adult use in 2018, and local decisions still determine whether a licensed store can open in a given town. This guide stays nonpartisan. It covers who decides what, how to register and vote in Michigan, and how to keep election night calm and legal.

Why elections matter for cannabis policy at every level

Cannabis law comes in layers, and every layer answers to elected officials or to voters directly.

  • Federal: Congress passed the Controlled Substances Act back in 1970, and federal agencies decide how cannabis is scheduled. As of October 2026, a federal regulation that took effect in April 2026 places marijuana-based medicines approved by the FDA, and marijuana covered by a state medical license, in Schedule III, while all other marijuana, including adult-use, remains in Schedule I. Further federal changes are possible, and our rescheduling explainer tracks them.
  • State: Michigan voters wrote the state's core cannabis laws. The Legislature and the Cannabis Regulatory Agency fill in details such as licensing, labels and taxes.
  • Local: City councils, village councils and township boards decide whether marijuana businesses may operate within their borders.

Courts shape the rules too, and Michigan's Supreme Court justices are elected on a nonpartisan ballot. In 2025, the court ruled that the smell of marijuana alone is no longer enough for police to search a vehicle. In 2026, it held that courts may not ban legal adult-use marijuana as a probation condition simply because it is illegal under federal law.

That is why races up and down the ballot, from Congress to the courts to your township board, can matter to people who care about cannabis, whichever way they lean.

Michigan's ballot history: the 2008 medical vote and the 2018 adult-use vote

Michigan's two biggest cannabis laws began as citizen-initiated ballot measures.

  • November 4, 2008: Voters approved the Michigan Medical Marihuana Act, which created the state's medical card program. The Cannabis Regulatory Agency runs it today.
  • November 6, 2018: Voters passed Proposal 1, which became the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act. It took effect December 6, 2018, allowing adults 21 and older to buy, possess and use cannabis, up to 2.5 ounces with no more than 15 grams of it as concentrate.

Both votes came after decades of prohibition, a story our war on drugs explainer tells in full. They also show what an initiative can do: when supporters gather enough valid signatures, voters can decide a law directly.

Who decides what: Congress, state law, city councils

LevelWho decidesWhat they controlExample
FederalCongress and federal agenciesDrug scheduling, interstate transport, federal landAn April 2026 regulation moved state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III; adult-use stays Schedule I
StateVoters, the Legislature and the Cannabis Regulatory AgencyWho can buy, possession limits, licensing, taxes, labelsThe 2018 voter-approved adult-use law
LocalCity, village and township governments, and local votersWhether stores may open, how many, signs and hoursLocal ordinances and ballot questions

The layers do not always agree. Adult-use cannabis is legal under Michigan law but still a Schedule I drug under federal law, which is why you cannot take it across state lines or onto federal land. Our guide to Michigan cannabis laws and our explainer on the Controlled Substances Act go deeper.

Local opt-ins and opt-outs: how towns decide where dispensaries open

Under the 2018 law, each Michigan city, village or township may ban marijuana businesses entirely or limit how many it allows. That is why licensed stores cluster in some communities and are missing from others. A municipality can also:

  • regulate the time, place and manner of operation, including signs
  • authorize designated consumption areas or limited special events
  • require a local license, with an annual fee of up to $5,000

What a town cannot do is stop people from transporting legal cannabis through it.

Because these choices are local, your city council or township board can shape cannabis access as much as any statewide race. Every licensed store, High Society's eight Michigan locations included, operates in a community that allows marijuana businesses.

How a local decision usually unfolds

  1. The council or board debates an ordinance that allows, caps or bans marijuana businesses.
  2. If it allows them, it sets local rules such as zoning, signs and hours, and decides whether to require a local license.
  3. Residents can weigh in at public meetings while the ordinance is under discussion.
  4. Sometimes residents take the question to voters directly, through a proposed initiated ordinance on the local ballot.

Whether you want stores in your town or not, those meetings and ballot questions are where the decision gets made.

Registering and voting in Michigan: deadlines, same-day registration, absentee and early voting

To vote in Michigan, you must be a U.S. citizen and a Michigan resident, be at least 18 by Election Day, and have lived in your city or township for at least 30 days by Election Day. These are the rules in place for Michigan's 2026 elections:

  • Register online or by mail up to 15 days before Election Day.
  • In the last 14 days, register in person at your city or township clerk's office, with proof of residency. Same-day registration runs until 8 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Vote absentee for any reason. Any registered voter may request an absentee ballot. Ballots are available 40 days before an election, and your clerk must receive yours by 8 p.m. on Election Day.
  • Vote early in person. Since 2024, Michigan has offered at least nine days of early, in-person voting before statewide elections, and some communities offer more.

You can check your registration, find your polling place and preview your sample ballot through the Michigan Voter Information Center or your local clerk.

Note: As of October 2026: Michigan's general election is Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Early voting runs at least October 24 through November 1. Requests to have an absentee ballot mailed to you are due by 5 p.m. Friday, October 30; after that, you can request one in person at your clerk's office until 4 p.m. Monday, November 2. Examples of cannabis questions on November 2026 ballots include one in the City of Bad Axe on whether to repeal its 2019 ban on marijuana establishments and allow up to two, and Massachusetts' Question 8 on repealing that state's laws legalizing, regulating and taxing cannabis. Your own sample ballot shows every local question.

Election day logistics

  • Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
  • Bring photo ID. If you do not have one, you can sign an affidavit and still vote a regular ballot.
  • Look up your polling place before you leave, since locations can change between elections.
  • Leave cannabis at home. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places, and if your polling place is a school, cannabis is not allowed on its grounds at all.
  • Plan your ride. Michigan has no numeric THC limit for drivers. It bans driving under the influence, and a separate zero-tolerance law bars driving with any amount of a Schedule 1 drug, a list that includes marijuana.

A calm, responsible election-night watch party

Counts can run late into the night and sometimes longer, so pace yourself. If you are hosting:

  • Keep it 21+. Keep infused food and drinks away from anyone under 21, and away from kids and pets entirely.
  • Share, do not sell. Michigan lets adults give up to 2.5 ounces, no more than 15 grams of it concentrate, to other adults 21 and older. Nothing may be received in return, and the gift may not be advertised or promoted to the public. Do not charge guests for cannabis.
  • Label everything infused, and put out plenty of non-infused snacks and drinks.
  • Go low and slow. Edible effects may not show for up to 2 hours, so do not stack doses while you wait on returns.
  • Skip the alcohol-and-cannabis combination, and line up rides or a couch for anyone who needs one.
  • Set friendly ground rules for politics talk, so the night stays fun whatever the outcome.

A simple host plan

WhenWhat to do
Before guests arriveLock up anything infused that is not being served, and label what is
Early eveningServe a real meal first, with infused options clearly marked and optional
As results come inKeep water, seltzer and alcohol-free drinks flowing; hold off on second doses
Late nightSet a cut-off for infused food so nobody is still waiting on an edible at midnight
Wrap-upCheck that everyone has a ride, and put labeled leftovers away out of reach

Want something on screen between results? A few classic election films fill the gaps: Mr. Smith Goes to Washington (1939), The Candidate (1972) and Election (1999).

Picking a mood for the night without health claims

Cannabis will not change a stressful news cycle, so choose based on how you like to feel at a gathering and what you know about your own tolerance:

  • Chatty and social: many people stay with a low dose, or a balanced THC:CBD product, dosed by its THC.
  • Low-key and cozy: a familiar product at your usual dose is a better bet than trying something new on a big night.
  • Flavor first: pick by aroma and taste, and let the label's THC number decide the dose.
  • Timing: inhaled cannabis is felt within minutes and edibles much later, so plan around when results usually come in.
  • Skipping it entirely: plenty of guests will not partake. Good alcohol-free and cannabis-free drinks mean nobody feels pressured either way.

Want a second opinion? Our budtenders are happy to answer questions and help you choose. Selection varies by store, so check with your nearest High Society store. Whatever you choose, vote first and celebrate later. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

How did Michigan legalize recreational marijuana?

By ballot initiative. Supporters put Proposal 1 on the November 2018 ballot, and voters approved it on November 6, 2018. It became the Michigan Regulation and Taxation of Marihuana Act, which took effect December 6, 2018, and lets adults 21 and older buy and carry as much as 2.5 ounces. Licensed adult-use stores opened in December 2019.

Can my city ban dispensaries in Michigan?

Yes. Under the 2018 law, every city, village and township may ban marijuana businesses or limit how many it allows, and it can regulate their time, place and manner of operation. What a town cannot do is restrict people from transporting legal cannabis through it. Local voters sometimes settle the question on the ballot.

Can I register to vote on Election Day in Michigan?

Yes. Online and mail registration close 15 days before the election, but you can register in person at your city or township clerk's office until 8 p.m. on Election Day. Bring proof of residency. In those final 14 days, registering in person at the clerk's office is the only option.

Is cannabis on the ballot this year?

That depends on your address. As of October 2026, examples on November ballots include a City of Bad Axe question on allowing up to two marijuana establishments and Massachusetts' Question 8 on repealing that state's adult-use laws. Your sample ballot, available through your local clerk, lists every question you will see.

Can I consume cannabis near a polling place?

Not in public. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places, and if your polling place is a school, cannabis is not allowed on its grounds at all. Vote first, then enjoy cannabis at home or on private property where it is permitted, and never before driving.

  4. U.S. Vote Foundation: Michigan voting requirements and 2026 datesusvotefoundation.org
  5. Bridge Michigan: 2026 Michigan voter guide (updated Oct. 5, 2026)bridgemi.com
  6. The Boston Globe: Massachusetts cannabis repeal question will be Question 8 on the Nov. 3 ballot (July 21, 2026)bostonglobe.com
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
